Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Check s-001 draft for (a) consistency with the plan and world rules: physical traces only, anchored ghost later, narrator reliable; (b) craft issues: opening should establish voice and habits, avoid passive closure, and not overshare future revelations. Look for any contradictions, missing provenance for the locket, unclear timestamps, or any statement implying retroactive alteration of documents. Focus on at most two craft blockers. Return an audit file path and verdict.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

After moving into a cheap room in an old house, a cautious young woman discovers the small, persistent traces of an eight‑year‑old who won't leave — and as she pieces together the child's life from locket, diary and marks in the attic, the house forces her to choose whether to confront the living truth kept under its floorboards or become another thing the walls keep.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-narrator: I — the first-person narrator, late twenties, recently divorced, moved into a cheap room to rebuild my life; cautious, curious, methodical, and compelled to keep a written record.
- char-mrs-hollis: Mrs. Hollis, the house's elderly landlady: small, precise, habit-bound, with clipped manners and a patient face whose civility barely conceals something worn and practiced.
- char-elsie: Elsie: an eight-year-old child who once lived in the house and left behind a cluster of small, physical traces (drawings, a locket). She is the ghost the narrator perceives — childlike in voice but capable of stubborn, repetitive action.
- loc-67-fairfax: 67 Fairfax: a narrow, three-story Victorian rental house with a variable smell of boiled tea and old paper; creaky stairs and thin walls. The house is a character in itself, with an attic that still smells of dust and varnish.
- loc-bedroom-2: The small upstairs room rented by the narrator: a single bed, a wardrobe, and a patch of wallpaper behind which something was once hidden. The room faces the alley and is colder at night.
- loc-attic: The low, angled attic space above the third floor; raw floorboards, exposed nails, boxes of forgotten possessions and a small trapdoor leading into the eaves.
- loc-hallway: The narrow central hallway running from the front door past the stairs: a thin runner, a faded portrait, and a clock that never keeps quite the right time.
- loc-kitchen: The communal kitchen on the ground floor: chipped sink, a table with four chairs, and shelves where Mrs. Hollis keeps jars of preserved fruit and a drawer of cheap tools.
- obj-silver-locket: A small, dented silver locket found tucked behind wallpaper in the narrator's room. Inside is a faded photograph and on the reverse, scratched initials.
- obj-sepia-photo: A sepia photograph, curled at the edges, showing a child (Elsie) with a broken toy. The picture's back has a pressed flower and a faint, smeared ink date.
- obj-diary: A thin, cloth-bound child's diary with childish handwriting, short dated entries, and a page torn out and folded into the back — the torn page's missing corner matches a scrap later found under a floorboard.
- obj-porcelain-doll: A small porcelain doll missing one eye; found in the attic, with a smear of dried mud on its dress and a braided ribbon tied to its wrist.
- obj-chalk: A handful of white chalk sticks for making marks on the attic floorboards and a jar stained with old handprints.
- obj-broken-clock: An old mantel clock in the hallway that stopped at a particular time and whose inner works bear a dent and a hairline scratch on the rim.
- obj-cracked-mirror: A narrow, wall-hung mirror in the bedroom with a single, hairline crack that distorts reflections along its lower edge.
- obj-floorboard-plank: A loose plank in the attic floor that covers a narrow cavity; when pried up it reveals a small stash of papers and a dark, stubborn stain on the subfloor beneath.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: first person, char-narrator, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Supernatural effects are bounded and leave physical, reproducible traces: scratches, displaced objects, marks on surfaces, temperature changes measurable by normal means.
- Ghosts in this story are anchored to people, objects, or places; they cannot teleport away from their anchor or create new anchors ex nihilo.
- No retroactive changes to recorded facts or documents: handwriting, photographs and stains found in the house were placed there in the past and cannot be altered by the ghost once discovered (the ghost can only reveal or reproduce marks consistent with existing materials).
- The narrator's perceptions are essentially reliable (senses, timestamps, recordings are trustworthy) though psychological tension can bias interpretation; contradictions must be resolvable by later, physical evidence.
- No time travel, no resurrection of the dead as living persons, and no physical impossibilities (e.g., objects do not pass through solid matter unless a consistent mechanism is supplied).
- Causality holds: every observed effect has a discoverable proximate cause within the world (possibly including the ghost's agency), and the reader should be able to follow the chain of reasoning from clue to conclusion.

10:12 a.m., March 3 — moved in.

I had parked the last box under the threadbare wardrobe and stood for a long minute in the doorway because 67 Fairfax folded around me like an old hand: the constant, faint smell of boiled tea and old paper, the stairs that complained in a different key with each step, and the thin walls that let the hall sound through as if it belonged to my room too. Mrs. Hollis met me on the landing with a key on a neat ribbon looped over one finger, small and exact as the woman who owned it.

She was exactly as you'd expect from her photographs in other people's mouths: small, precise, habit-bound. She inclined her head once, clipped the name from my lips, and ticked off rules in sentences that behaved like lists.

"No smoking in the house, please. No late visitors up past eleven. And don't be troubled by the hall clock — it's been stopped since before my time; there's nothing to be done about it."

It was the way she said it — the civility with an edge of practised reluctance — that made me ask, before I could be polite, whether we'd met before. "No," she said, with a quick, patient smile that folded thought away. "This is the first proper time."

11:03 a.m. — I wrote the hour in my notebook as habit demanded, because writing things down made them smaller, manageable. Mrs. Hollis showed me where I could put the kettle and pointed at the hallway with the same clipped hand: "Don't worry about it; the clock's stopped at 4:22, it likes that time."

I noted the stopped face of the broken clock as she mentioned it and then shut the door on the landing's soft light. My room was smaller than I expected: a single bed, a narrow wardrobe, a wall-hung mirror with a hairline crack low on its glass, and a strip of floral wallpaper behind the wardrobe where someone had made a patch.

The patch was fresher than the rest of the wall: its edge had the clean, un-aged line of a recent glue job. Behind the wardrobe, in the right-hand corner where the paper had been tucked and folded by a careful thumb, there was a narrow gap beneath the lining.

I shifted the wardrobe and my fingers went into that seam without thinking. It gave like a mouth and something small and silver slid against my knuckle — cold with dust.

11:07 a.m. — found silver locket.

The locket was dented on one side, its chain run through with the almost-absence of a loop. A smear ran along the rim, red-brown in the way rust leans and dark like dried mud, so I turned it over on the palm of my hand as if it might explain itself.

When I prised it open the photograph inside was a faded sepia: a child with a broken toy held in both hands, the edges curled and soft. On the reverse, two letters had been scratched clumsily into the silver — E.L. — shallow enough that dust sat in the grooves. The whole piece smelled faintly of old soap and a hint of lavender; a scatter of powder dusted the hinge.

I held the locket up to the mirror. The hairline crack distorted the lower third of the reflection so the dented edge of the locket seemed doubled, as if two small mouths were making a secret of the photograph between them.

I put the locket into my pocket and wrote it down, because if the house kept things, I would keep a record of them too.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.

- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.

- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.

    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"

    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- Supernatural effects are bounded and leave physical, reproducible traces: scratches, displaced objects, marks on surfaces, temperature changes measurable by normal means.
- Ghosts in this story are anchored to people, objects, or places; they cannot teleport away from their anchor or create new anchors ex nihilo.
- No retroactive changes to recorded facts or documents: handwriting, photographs and stains found in the house were placed there in the past and cannot be altered by the ghost once discovered (the ghost can only reveal or reproduce marks consistent with existing materials).

"No smoking in the house, please. No late visitors up past eleven. And don't be troubled by the hall clock — it's been stopped since before my time; there's nothing to be done about it."

It was the way she said it — the civility with an edge of practised reluctance — that made me ask, before I could be polite, whether we'd met before. "No," she said, with a quick, patient smile that folded thought away. "This is the first proper time."

11:03 a.m. — I wrote the hour in my notebook as habit demanded, because writing things down made them smaller, manageable. The patch was fresher than the rest of the wall: its edge had the clean, un-aged line of a recent glue job. Behind the wardrobe, in the right-hand corner where the paper had been tucked and folded by a careful thumb, there was a narrow gap beneath the lining.

I shifted the wardrobe and my fingers went into that seam without thinking. It gave like a mouth and something small and silver slid against my knuckle — cold with dust.

11:07 a.m. — found silver locket.

The locket was dented on one side, its chain run through with the almost-absence of a loop. A smear ran along the rim, red-brown in the way rust leans and dark like dried mud, so I turned it over on the palm of my hand as if it might explain itself. The silver and the way it had been dented looked almost a century old — early twentieth century; the metal was worn thin at the edges in a way the chain, barely there, did not match.

When I prised it open the photograph inside was a faded sepia: a child with a broken toy held in both hands, the edges curled and soft. On the reverse, two letters had been scratched clumsily into the silver — E.L. — shallow enough that dust sat in the grooves. The whole piece smelled faintly of old soap and a hint of lavender; a scatter of powder dusted the hinge.

I held the locket up to the mirror. The hairline crack distorted the lower third of the reflection so the dented edge of the locket seemed doubled, as if two small mouths were making a secret of the photograph between them.

I slipped the locket into my pocket and, without thinking, wrote a quick line in my notebook: "11:07 — silver locket. E.L."

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:

  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

10:12 a.m., March 3 — moved in.

I had parked the last box under the threadbare wardrobe and stood for a long minute in the doorway because 67 Fairfax folded around me like an old hand: the constant, faint smell of boiled tea and old paper, the stairs that complained in a different key with each step, and the thin walls that let the hall sound through as if it belonged to my room too. Mrs. Hollis met me on the landing with a key on a neat ribbon looped over one finger, small and exact as the woman who owned it.

She was exactly as you'd expect from her photographs in other people's mouths: small, precise, habit-bound. She inclined her head once, clipped the name from my lips, and ticked off rules in sentences that behaved like lists.

"No smoking in the house, please. No late visitors up past eleven. And don't be troubled by the hall clock — it's been stopped since before my time; there's nothing to be done about it."

It was the way she said it — the civility with an edge of practised reluctance — that made me ask, before I could be polite, whether we'd met before. "No," she said, with a quick, patient smile that folded thought away. "This is the first proper time."

11:03 a.m. — I wrote the hour in my notebook as habit demanded, because writing things down made them smaller, manageable. Mrs. Hollis showed me where I could put the kettle and pointed at the hallway with the same clipped hand: "Don't worry about it; the clock's stopped at 4:22, it likes that time."

I noted the stopped face of the broken clock as she mentioned it and then shut the door on the landing's soft light. My room was smaller than I expected: a single bed, a narrow wardrobe, a wall-hung mirror with a hairline crack low on its glass, and a strip of floral wallpaper behind the wardrobe where someone had made a patch.

The patch was fresher than the rest of the wall: its edge had the clean, un-aged line of a recent glue job. Behind the wardrobe, in the right-hand corner where the paper had been tucked and folded by a careful thumb, there was a narrow gap beneath the lining.

I shifted the wardrobe and my fingers went into that seam without thinking. It gave like a mouth and something small and silver slid against my knuckle — cold with dust.

11:07 a.m. — found silver locket.

The locket was dented on one side, its chain run through with the almost-absence of a loop. A smear ran along the rim, red-brown in the way rust leans and dark like dried mud, so I turned it over on the palm of my hand as if it might explain itself. The silver and the way it had been dented looked almost a century old — early twentieth century; the metal was worn thin at the edges in a way the chain, barely there, did not match.

When I prised it open the photograph inside was a faded sepia: a child with a broken toy held in both hands, the edges curled and soft. On the reverse, two letters had been scratched clumsily into the silver — E.L. — shallow enough that dust sat in the grooves. The whole piece smelled faintly of old soap and a hint of lavender; a scatter of powder dusted the hinge.

I held the locket up to the mirror. The hairline crack distorted the lower third of the reflection so the dented edge of the locket seemed doubled, as if two small mouths were making a secret of the photograph between them.

I slipped the locket into my pocket and, without thinking, wrote a quick line in my notebook: "11:07 — silver locket. E.L."

The next morning I climbed up the narrow ladder to the attic with a torch and my notebook in my breast pocket. 9:14 a.m. — attic. Cold light came through the gable and the whole place smelled of dust and old varnish. The trapdoor had a crescent of white on the hinge: damp chalk smudges, the chalk itself soft to the touch as if it had been pressed and rubbed minutes, not years, ago. A jar on a low crate wore pale handprints around its rim where someone had held it; the powder on the prints still felt faintly tacky when I brushed at it with a fingertip.

I moved a tea tin that had been balanced like an afterthought on the central joist and there, under its dented lid, the doll lay on its side. 9:21 a.m. — porcelain doll. It had one glass eye gone; the socket stared with an empty glaze. A braided ribbon was knotted to its wrist and a smear of dried mud darkened the hem of its dress. The doll smelled like attic dust and something faintly of garden earth. I set it on my palm and its small porcelain head swung as if someone had just breathed near it.

Along the northern eaves I found the diary wedged tight under a beam where the rafters met the floor. 9:26 a.m. — diary and drawing. The cloth cover was frayed and the handwriting was small, earnest and a little slanted. Short entries, dates in a child’s hand; one page had a drawing of a toy with a bent wheel that looked, at a glance, like the broken toy in the photograph I had opened in the locket. At the back a page had been torn out and the torn corner folded back into the lining like a secret.

Three boards from the trapdoor the floor was slightly springy. I levered the loose plank and the edge came up with a greyed sigh. 9:33 a.m. — floorboard plank. The cavity beneath held a narrow bundle of papers and envelopes the size of a child's palm; beneath them the subfloor bore a dark, stubborn stain. The stain was dry when I touched it — a dark patch that smelled faintly of iron and old cloth, as if something had bled and then been left to the dust. I photographed it quickly with my phone and wrote the time down.

Everything in that attic behaved like evidence. The chalk at the trapdoor hinge was damp; the jar had thumbprints in white powder; the joists carried the exact cadence of footfalls into the bedroom below. Nothing looked staged, nothing supernatural in the theatrical sense — only small, repeatable marks that a child might have made and, for reasons that did not yet make sense, continued to make.

I sat on the floor with the doll in one hand and the diary open on my knees, the locket warm against my palm where I had taken it out to compare the bent wheel in the drawing to the photograph inside it. The bent toy in the picture and the child's scrawl in the diary matched close enough that I could not dismiss the likeness. And the smear along the locket's rim stayed unexplained, a dark comma I had not yet read.

9:48 a.m. — I wrote the time and the feeling: a small presence, patient and precise, and an anxiety that had the shape of a clock hand moving steadily toward something I could not yet name.

Summary

I ran the draft against the packet, the scene card and the world rules. The deterministic checks already showed no schema or direct canon conflicts; the scene does what its card asked (attic exploration, reproducible traces, findspots, diary + doll + floorboard discovered) and it advances the plot promises without contradicting the index.

I filed one finding (a consistency warning). Nothing else required blocking repair.

Recorded finding (what I wrote into the dossier)

- Subtype: causeless_effects (warning)
- Where: draft — novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md
- Offending quote (draft): "I set it on my palm and its small porcelain head swung as if someone had just breathed near it."
- Why: As written the doll's motion reads like an unexplained, momentary movement that implies agency without a proximate, physical cause. World rules require supernatural effects to leave physical, reproducible traces and for causality to hold: every observed effect must have a discoverable proximate cause or be demonstrably repeatable. The sentence risks implying a causeless or purely perceptual effect rather than one that other characters or a later examination could verify.
- Canon context (quoted): "Supernatural effects are bounded and leave physical, reproducible traces: scratches, displaced objects, marks on surfaces, temperature changes measurable by normal means. Ghosts in this story are anchored to people, objects, or places; they cannot teleport away from their anchor or create new anchors ex nihilo. Causality holds: every observed effect has a discoverable proximate cause within the world (possibly including the ghost's agency), and the reader should be able to follow the chain of reasoning from clue to conclusion." — world/rules.yaml
- Severity: warning
- Suggestion: Make the doll's motion explicitly physical or demonstrably repeatable. Options:
  - Give a concrete proximate cause in one short clause (e.g., "as a draft came through the gable," "the knot of the ribbon caught and released," "its neck joint, loose from years of being handled"); or
  - Show reproducibility: rub or nudge the doll and note that the head swings the same way, set it on a flat surface and photograph its before/after positions, or observe that the head swings when the narrator breathes on it and then again when she taps the board — that makes the motion a measurable, repeatable effect rather than an anomalous, causeless twitch.
I recorded the finding to the draft; it is a warning rather than an error, because it can be fixed with a short clarifying line and does not block the scene.

Other observations and recommendations (not filed as findings)

- The scene fulfills the scene-card intent: the attic yields precise, physical traces (damp chalk at the trapdoor hinge, tacky jar handprints, doll under the tea tin, diary wedged under the eaves, loose plank with stash). Findspots are concrete and appropriately detailed; timestamps and the narrator's notebook habit link the scene to the previous one as required.
- Promises from s-001:
  - pr-01 (photograph provenance / match to obj-sepia-photo): this scene supplies a useful connective beat — the diary drawing's bent wheel "matched close enough" to the photograph in the locket — but it does not yet supply full provenance or a clear, named match to the separate object obj-sepia-photo (if that was intended). If the orchestrator expected an explicit link to obj-sepia-photo, the writer should either:
    - make explicit that the locket photograph is the same as obj-sepia-photo (quote or describe a unique, verifiable detail common to both), or
    - leave the partial match as an intentional hint and defer full provenance to a later scene. If the former is intended, add one line making the match explicit (e.g., "the broken toy in the locket was the same one in the sepia photograph tucked among the boxes — the bent wheel matched exactly").
  - pr-02 (smear analysis): the scene explicitly leaves the locket smear unresolved, which is an honest state; that promise remains unpaid and is noted in continuity. That's fine — don't invent an analysis here unless the scene is meant to pay it off.
- Voice / tense: consistent first-person past. Notebook timestamps work well as connective tissue with s-001.
- Pacing / craft: the scene is a bit longer than target (709 vs ~625) but the additional words carry discovery beats rather than padding; no "nothing_changes" or "restates_prior_scene" problems detected. If anything, the prose could tighten one or two phrases, but that's a stylistic note, not a correctness problem.

If you want, I can:
- File a craft note suggesting one sentence to make the photograph-diary linkage explicit (if you intend to pay pr-01 here).
- Or produce suggested rewrites for the single line about the doll swinging so you can drop one into the draft quickly.

Verdict: scene passes with one small, fixable warning (doll motion should be explicitly physical or reproducible).
